opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so before Epoch I was doing research on the economics of computing and machine learning, partly in academic settings, and what I kept running into was a mismatch between the questions I thought mattered most and the incentives of the places where I could work on them. In academia, you're rewarded for producing papers that fit neatly into an existing literature and that referees in a particular field recognize as a contribution. But the questions I cared about, like how fast compute is scaling, how much algorithmic progress contributes relative to hardware, what the trajectory of AI capabilities looks like over the next decade or two, don't sit cleanly in any one discipline. They're part economics, part computer science, part forecasting, and a lot of it is just careful, somewhat unglamorous data work.

That data work was a big part of it. A lot of what's actually useful for understanding AI progress is building datasets: tracking training compute for notable models, documenting hardware price-performance, estimating how much more efficient algorithms have become. That kind of work is enormously valuable as a public good, but it's very hard to get credit for in a traditional academic career. Nobody gets tenure for maintaining a well-curated database of training runs.

At the same time, I didn't think the frontier labs were the right home for it either. They have a lot of the relevant information, but they also have commercial incentives, and their research is often not public or is shaped by what they want to communicate. I thought there was real value in having an independent group whose whole job was to give an honest, evidence-based picture of where AI is heading, and to make that available to policymakers, researchers, and the public.

So starting Epoch was a way to build an institution around exactly that set of questions. We could hire people with a mix of backgrounds, focus on the empirical foundations, publish things quickly when they were useful rather than waiting on a journal cycle, and take on long, slow projects that wouldn't make sense anywhere else. And there was a sense that this was neglected: a lot of people were making strong claims about AI timelines and impacts, and comparatively few were doing the grounded, quantitative work to check them. That gap felt like an opportunity where a small, focused team could have a disproportionate impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that when I was doing this work before, first at MIT and then at other places, I kept running into this problem where the questions I actually cared about didn't fit neatly into any existing institution. I was interested in things like, how fast is compute actually scaling? How much do algorithmic improvements matter relative to just throwing more hardware at the problem? What does the trajectory of AI look like if you take the trends seriously and extrapolate them? And these are sort of empirical, almost economic-history-flavored questions about AI, and academia didn't really reward that. You'd write a paper on compute trends and the reviewers would say, well, this is interesting, but what's the contribution? Where's the theorem, where's the new method?

And the labs, on the other hand, had a lot of the relevant knowledge, but they weren't particularly incentivized to publish it, and in many cases couldn't. So there was this gap where some of the most decision-relevant information about where AI was going just wasn't being collected and made public in any systematic way.

So the pitch for Epoch was basically: let's just build the thing that we wished existed. Collect the data on training runs, on compute, on hardware, on datasets, put it out publicly, and do the kind of careful forecasting work that nobody else seemed to be set up to do. And I think the independence mattered a lot. We weren't trying to sell anything, we weren't trying to get tenure, so we could just follow the questions wherever they led, and that turned out to be a much better fit for what I wanted to do than trying to shoehorn it into a PhD or a lab research agenda.

astra-6.text:
I wanted to work on questions about where AI was going that didn’t fit particularly neatly into an existing academic field. How quickly were the inputs to AI progressing? How much compute were people using, how much data, and what could that tell us about future capabilities?

A lot of that work required building the empirical foundation yourself—collecting data, checking estimates, and maintaining datasets. That’s useful work, but it doesn’t always line up with the incentives to publish a novel academic result. Starting Epoch seemed like a way to make those questions the central priority and bring together people who wanted to work on them.

There was also the freedom to change direction as we learned things. Rather than committing to a particular method or discipline, we could start with a question we thought mattered and then figure out what kind of research would actually help answer it.

sol-6.1.text:
I wanted to work on empirical questions about where AI is going: how quickly the inputs to progress are growing, what constraints we might run into, and what that implies for the capabilities we should expect. Those questions seemed very important, but there wasn’t an obvious institutional home for doing that work systematically.

The attraction of starting Epoch was that we could make those questions the central agenda. We could build datasets, invest in the infrastructure needed to keep them updated, and bring together people with different skills to work on a shared picture of AI progress.

That’s a little different from pursuing individual papers. You want each project to contribute to something cumulative: a better understanding of what’s driving progress and how far those drivers might take us. Having an organization focused on that seemed like a good way to do the research I was excited about.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains why Besiroglu wanted Epoch to pursue cumulative empirical research, but it does not mention his MIT principal investigator or publication prospects or prestige as a reason for differing enthusiasm.
